searchLog.searched: 2026-11-02: FSI Insights 35 and 63, BCBS 2018, BCBS 2022 newsletter, BCBS 2024; grep existing (requirements|frameworks)|technology.neutral|AI-specific.
searchLog.earliestNote: FSI Insights 35 (August 2021). BCBS 2018 Implication 9 concerns fintech generally, not AI; not recorded. The BCBS newsletter (2022) says supervisors and banks are assessing whether existing practices remain sufficient (not recorded). Contesting: FSI Insights 63 (partial).

searchLog.searched: Proudman (2019); BoE–FCA survey (2019, technology-neutral box); DP5/22; FS2/23; Wuermeling (2022); Breeden (2024, 2026); Machado (2026); ECB FSR 2024; Räsänen (2024); BoE innovation report (2025, technology-agnostic box). DNB general principles (2019) refused (HTTP 403).
searchLog.earliestNote: Proudman (4 June 2019) is the earliest articulation found. The 2019 survey states that supervisors are technology neutral but does not say existing frameworks suffice and is not recorded. Breeden (30 June 2026) is the only contesting text found.

searchLog.searched: All texts grepped for technology-neutral, technology neutral, existing (regulat*|framework*|legislation|rules), new requirements, AI-specific; FSB Chair speech and letter; EIOPA Opinion 2025.
searchLog.earliestNote: Chapter 3 of the IMF GFSR of October 2024 is the earliest text found that states existing frameworks are technology-neutral and applicable to AI. The Knot speech of July 2024 is earlier but speaks of frameworks to assess risks and is recorded as context. The IMF Departmental Paper of 2021 relays that some jurisdictions concluded existing rules suffice, but its authors contest the proposition. Contesting texts: IMF Departmental Paper 2021; ESRB ASC Report No 16 (2025).

searchLog.searched: Grep for 'existing', 'technology-neutral', 'framework' with 'AI' in retrieved texts; Brainard 2018; Bowman 2024; interagency RFI 2021; PBoC 2019 and 2022-2025 plans; MAS FEAT 2018, MindForge whitepaper, AIRM consultation 2025; HKMA 2019 principles; RBI FREE-AI report; Ueda 2024; Waller Oct 2025.
searchLog.earliestNote: Brainard (13 November 2018) is the earliest articulation found. The PBoC plan (August 2019) is the earliest contesting text found (contrary-only); the RBI FREE-AI report (August 2025) engages the premise. Ueda (21 November 2024) says current financial regulations may not be fully equipped for new types of financial services from technology generally, not AI specifically (not recorded).

statement: In remarks of 13 April 2017, Haruhiko Kuroda, Governor of the Bank of Japan, said that there are concerns that high-frequency and algorithmic trading may increase market volatility, especially if massive trading is based on a similar algorithm, and that applying AI and big data analytics to such trading might intensify these effects.
qualification: A conditional statement in opening remarks: the concern about similar algorithms is reported as one side of an argument, and the speaker's own claim is that AI 'might intensify' it. Not evidence that such effects occurred; the remarks do not state a Bank of Japan position.

evidence.locator: Section on new issues for market stakeholders and policymakers, paragraph beginning 'High-frequency trading (HFT) and algorithmic trading'
evidence.passage: At the same time, there are also concerns that HFT and algorithmic trading may increase market volatility, especially if massive trading is based on a similar algorithm
As such, the application of AI and big data analytics to HFT and algorithmic trading might intensify these negative impacts.

statement: The FSB report of 1 November 2017 states that the lack of interpretability or auditability of AI and machine-learning methods could become a macro-level risk if not appropriately supervised, and that widespread use of opaque models would make it very difficult for firms and supervisors to predict how model-directed actions affect markets.
qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy.

evidence.passage: The lack of interpretability or ‘auditability’ of AI and machine learning methods has the potential to contribute to macro-level risk if not appropriately supervised by microprudential supervisors.
it would be very difficult for both firms and supervisors to predict how actions directed by models will affect markets.

statement: In a Euro & talous analysis of 5 September 2024 published by the Bank of Finland, economist Tatu Räsänen writes (in Finnish) that the spread of generative AI has already increased risks linked to cyber threats, information operations and fraud, that deepfakes make fraud easier, and that generative AI enables more sophisticated cyberattacks.
qualification: Quoted in the original Finnish; English paraphrase in the evidence notes. The article cites a US Treasury report for these points and carries a disclaimer that the views are the author’s. It states risk channels, not measured losses.

evidence.locator: Section “Generatiivisen tekoälyn yleistyminen voi lisätä epävakauttaviin kehityskulkuihin liittyviä riskejä rahoitussektorilla”, first paragraph
evidence.passage: Generatiivisen tekoälyn yleistyminen on jo lisännyt kybermaailmaan, informaatiovaikuttamiseen ja huijauksiin liittyviä riskejä.
evidence.note: English paraphrase: the spread of generative AI has already increased risks related to the cyber domain, information operations and scams.

evidence.passage: Huijauksista ja disinformaation levittämisestä on tullut yhä helpompia toteuttaa edistyksellisten syväväärennösten (deepfake) avulla. Tämän ohella generatiivinen tekoäly mahdollistaa sofistikoituneempien kyberhyökkäysten toteuttamisen.
evidence.note: English paraphrase: scams and the spreading of disinformation have become ever easier to carry out with advanced deepfakes; in addition, generative AI enables more sophisticated cyberattacks.

statement: FSI Insights No 35 of August 2021, by Jermy Prenio and Jeffery Yong, states that existing requirements on governance, risk management and traditional models also apply to AI models, and that most issues arising from AI use are similar to those for traditional models.
qualification: A staff paper under the FSI series disclaimer. The same summary also states that there is scope for standard-setting bodies to develop international guidance on AI and calls for a proportional regulatory response.

evidence.passage: Existing requirements on governance, risk management, as well as development and operation of traditional models also apply to AI models.
While most of the issues arising from the use of AI by financial institutions are similar to those for traditional models, the perspective might be different.

engagement.rationale: The box disputes the premise that AI use makes trading decisions more alike, holding that it may instead diversify trading signals, and questions that correlated trading has been harmful.

statement: The Federal Reserve Board's Financial Stability Report of November 2025 (Box 1.1) states that AI may also help reduce the likelihood of correlated trade execution, by allowing richer information and more complex logic and so a greater diversity of trading signals, and that historical evidence suggests correlated algorithmic trading has not necessarily been detrimental to market quality.
qualification: The same box also relays the concern ('a long-standing concern', 'cannot be dismissed') and calls for continued monitoring; the contest is partial and balanced within one text. It is the Board's report, not evidence about market outcomes.

evidence.locator: Box 1.1 'Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Trading', PDF p. 23 (printed p. 15), paragraph 3
evidence.passage: That said, the use of AI may also help reduce the likelihood of correlated trade execution, as it facilitates the use of richer information and more complex logic, potentially leading to a less uniform response to news and to a greater diversity of trading signals among market participants.

evidence.locator: Box 1.1, closing paragraph, PDF p. 24 (printed p. 16)
evidence.passage: historical evidence from algorithmic trading suggests that correlated trading has not necessarily been detrimental to market quality.

evidence.locator: Box 1.1, closing paragraph, PDF p. 24 (printed p. 16)
evidence.passage: While the potential for AI to increase correlated trading and impact market competition cannot be dismissed
evidence.note: The box keeps the concern open.

statement: Chapter 3 of the IMF Global Financial Stability Report of October 2024, prepared by IMF staff, states that AI models and related IT services reside with a handful of key providers and that, if capital markets become too reliant on them, the failure of these providers may lead to market stress akin to the failure of key financial market utilities.
qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The chapter also reports that participants in the IMF outreach cited vendor concentration as a potential source of systemic risk (a relay of outreach views, given as context).

evidence.locator: Section "Summarizing the Financial Stability Challenges", "Increased operational risks as a result of reliance on a few key third-party AI service providers" (HTML)
evidence.passage: AI models and related information technology services currently reside with a handful of key providers with dominant computational power and established large language models.

If capital markets activities become too reliant on these models, the failure of these providers may lead to market stress akin to the failure of key financial market utilities such as clearing houses.

statement: In remarks of 4 November 1997, Susan M. Phillips, Governor of the Federal Reserve Board, said that some institutions are making significant strides to better quantify and manage credit risk, including through credit scoring and the use of artificial intelligence in underwriting various types of consumer loans.
qualification: A single mention within a list of credit-risk developments; the speech does not describe how AI improves underwriting or assess its effect. Located through Governor Barr's citation of it (speech of 11 November 2025); a citation is not agreement or influence.

evidence.locator: Section 'Increased Use of Internal Measurement and Management Systems', paragraph beginning 'Moving forward, perhaps such supervisory/private sector synergies'
evidence.passage: At present, some institutions are making significant strides on a number of fronts to better quantify and manage credit risk. In addition to major developments in credit scoring and the use of artificial intelligence in underwriting various types of consumer loans

statement: BIS Working Paper No 930 of March 2021, by Sebastian Doerr, Leonardo Gambacorta and Jose Maria Serena, reports that several central banks face constraints in IT infrastructure and human capital for big data and machine learning, and states that cooperation among public authorities could improve central banks' ability to collect, store and analyse big data.
qualification: A staff working paper under its disclaimer, drawing on an IFC survey. Its subject is big data used with machine learning, not AI generally.

evidence.passage: Several institutions report constraints in setting up an adequate IT infrastructure and in developing the necessary human capital. Cooperation among public authorities could improve central banks' ability to collect, store and analyse big data.

statement: In Bank of England Staff Working Paper No. 674 of September 2017, Chiranjit Chakraborty and Andreas Joseph introduce machine learning for central banking and policy analysis, present a case study projecting UK CPI inflation, and write that machine-learning models generally outperform traditional approaches in prediction tasks.
qualification: A staff working paper with the authors’ disclaimer; the authors also state that open questions remain about causal inference. Their result is from their own case studies, not an adopted forecasting practice.

evidence.passage: We introduce machine learning in the context of central banking and policy analyses.
Machine learning models generally outperform traditional modelling approaches in prediction tasks, while open research questions remain with regard to their causal inference properties.

missing: The passage does not name AI or machine-learning models; it concerns robo-advice and social trading algorithms generally.
statement: The FSB report of 27 June 2017 on financial stability implications from FinTech states that social trading and robo-advice could show greater herding behaviour than traditional portfolio allocation if risk models are highly correlated through reliance on similar algorithms, and notes that it found no empirical evidence so far of convergence of robo-advisors’ algorithms or portfolios.
qualification: The passage concerns robo-advice and social trading algorithms; it does not name AI or machine learning (the report’s glossary says robo-advisors "can also include machine learning"). Recorded as context to the November 2017 articulation.

evidence.locator: Section 3 (financial stability risks), PDF p. 24 (printed p. 20)
evidence.passage: Social trading and robo-advice could potentially exhibit greater herding behaviour than traditional portfolio allocation methods – for example, if risk models are highly correlated due to reliance on similar algorithms – thereby potentially increasing the amplitude of swings in asset prices.
we found no empirical evidence so far on convergence of robo-advisors’ algorithms or portfolios.

statement: The FSB report of 27 June 2017 on financial stability implications from FinTech states, in its case study on AI and machine learning, that key risks include the opacity and lack of auditability of "black box" algorithms, and that the auditability of AI models used by banks might be difficult to achieve given model validation practices that require models to be explained to regulators.
qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The annex describes its findings as preliminary.

evidence.locator: Annex G "Case study on AI and machine learning", "Potential to undermine financial stability", PDF p. 60 (printed p. 56)
evidence.passage: Key risks include the opacity and lack of auditability of algorithms (in case of “black boxes”) and undesired changes to market structure.
Specifically, the “auditability” of the models might be difficult to achieve and not ensured in all cases.

statement: In a keynote address of 14 October 2024, Shaktikanta Das, Governor of the Reserve Bank of India, said that heavy reliance on AI can lead to concentration risks, especially when a small number of tech providers dominate the market, and that failures or disruptions in these systems may cascade across the entire financial sector.
qualification: One paragraph of a keynote on central banking; the speaker's statement of a possible risk, not evidence that such a disruption has occurred, and not an RBI regulatory measure.

evidence.passage: The heavy reliance on AI can lead to concentration risks, especially when a small number of tech providers dominate the market. This could amplify systemic risks, as failures or disruptions in these systems may cascade across the entire financial sector.

statement: The FSB report of 14 November 2024 states that the complexity and limited explainability of some AI methods, and the difficulty of assessing data quality for widely used models, could increase model risk for financial institutions lacking robust AI governance.
qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy.

evidence.locator: Executive summary, "Model risk, data quality and governance", PDF pp. 5–6 (printed pp. 1–2)
evidence.passage: The complexity and limited explainability of some AI methods and the difficulty of assessing data quality for widely used AI models … could increase model risk for FIs that lack robust AI governance.
evidence.note: The ellipsis marks only the page break between PDF pp. 5 and 6 (page number and footer); no words of the sentence are omitted.

statement: In a speech of 22 September 2023, Lisa D. Cook, Governor of the Federal Reserve Board, said that she focuses on AI as a monetary policymaker because of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate, and that the impact of AI on the economy and monetary policy will depend on whether it is a general purpose technology.
qualification: The speaker's view with disclaimer; it links AI's productivity and labour-market effects to the dual mandate but proposes no policy response. Bowman (22 November 2024) and later speeches restate the link.

evidence.locator: Introduction, paragraph beginning 'Why do I focus on AI as a monetary policymaker?'
evidence.passage: Why do I focus on AI as a monetary policymaker? The Federal Reserve's dual mandate is to promote maximum employment and stable prices.
The impact of AI on the economy and monetary policy will depend on whether AI is just another app or something more profound.

missing: The passage names 羊群效应 (herding effect) as an algorithm problem to be prevented but does not state the mechanism (similar models or data making decisions alike) or that it could amplify shocks or volatility.
statement: The People's Bank of China's FinTech Development Plan 2022–2025, issued by notice of 29 December 2021, lists the herding effect (羊群效应), together with the algorithmic black box and algorithmic discrimination, among problems that financial institutions are to guard against through stress testing, simulation and parameter tuning.
qualification: A planning document's task list in Chinese; the English rendering is a paraphrase. It records that the plan names the problem, not that herding has occurred or that measures were implemented.

evidence.locator: Attachment, chapter on tasks, item （二十四）筑牢金融与科技风险防火墙
evidence.passage: 通过临界测试、仿真模拟、参数调优等方式着力防范算法黑盒、羊群效应、算法歧视等问题，提升算法可解释性、透明性、公平性和安全性。
evidence.note: English paraphrase: through critical testing, simulation and parameter tuning, guard against problems such as the algorithmic black box, the herding effect and algorithmic discrimination, and raise the explainability, transparency, fairness and security of algorithms.

statement: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's circular of 9 September 2024 states that the HKMA observes that AI-powered suspicious-activity monitoring systems adopted by some authorized institutions have proved more effective and efficient than conventional rules-based transaction monitoring.
qualification: The HKMA's observation of some institutions' systems, stated in a circular that also asks institutions with significant operations to study adoption; it publishes no comparative data in the letter.

evidence.locator: Letter, page 1, paragraph beginning 'The HKMA shared a list of high-level principles'
evidence.passage: These enhanced systems have proved to be more effective and efficient than conventional rules-based transaction monitoring systems commonly used by AIs.
evidence.note: 'AIs' in the circular means Authorized Institutions.

missing: Names financial stability as an area for analysis but states no mechanism of correlated or herding behaviour.
statement: The Basel Committee's newsletter of 16 March 2022 on AI and machine learning states that its continuing discussions will cover the potential implications of broader usage of AI/ML models for the resilience of individual banks and for financial stability.
qualification: The newsletter states it is for information only and is not supervisory guidance.

evidence.locator: Third of the three areas listed for continuing discussions
evidence.passage: The third area named for continuing discussions is the potential implications of broader usage of AI/ML models for the resilience of individual banks and, more broadly, for financial stability.

statement: The FSB final report of 15 October 2026 on sound practices for responsible AI adoption states that the FSB and relevant standard-setting bodies emphasise proportionate, risk-based and technology-neutral approaches, and that its sound practices are non-binding and can be integrated into existing frameworks.
qualification: The report also notes that some standard-setting bodies have issued AI-specific guidance and that some risks of agentic AI are newer; the record does not show that no AI-specific rules exist or are needed.

evidence.passage: The FSB and relevant SSBs emphasise proportionate, risk‑based and technology‑neutral approaches to monitoring and addressing risks
The sound practices are non-prescriptive and do not constitute a binding international standard.

statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2025 (chapter III) states that machine learning tools present opportunities to help combat financial crime, reducing false positives and increasing detection of fraudulent transactions.
qualification: Concerns AML/CFT compliance; Box B also describes AI agents as possible co-pilots in preparing suspicious activity reports.

evidence.locator: Section 'Stablecoins and the integrity imperative', paragraph beginning 'Technological improvements can enhance the integrity'
evidence.passage: AI and data integration advances, particularly through the development of machine learning tools, present opportunities to help combat financial crime. These innovations help reduce false positives (ie legitimate transactions flagged as illicit) and increase detection of fraudulent transactions.

statement: In the Whitaker Lecture of 14 September 2018, Mark Carney, Governor of the Bank of England, said that “the appropriate setting of monetary policy will be influenced by” the structural changes of a Fourth Industrial Revolution, which he described as driven by advances in AI, automation and interconnectedness, including through the labour market, price dynamics and the equilibrium rate of interest.
qualification: The speech speaks of a “Fourth Industrial Revolution” of which AI is one named component, not of AI alone. It states an expected influence on policy, not a policy decision.

evidence.passage: We are on the cusp of a Fourth Industrial Revolution, which has the potential to transform fundamentally the nature of both work and commerce through advances in AI, automation and interconnectedness.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 10, section “Monetary Policy’s Role in Managing the Transition”
evidence.passage: The appropriate setting of monetary policy will be influenced by the structural changes wrought by the Fourth Industrial Revolution, including in the labour market, by its impact on price dynamics and on the equilibrium rate of interest.

statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2024 (chapter III) states that AI will affect productivity, consumption, investment and labour markets, which have direct effects on price and financial stability, and that these developments are of paramount concern to central banks.
qualification: States relevance for central bank mandates; the chapter's section on macroeconomic effects presents scenarios in which AI's initial effect on inflation could be disinflationary or inflationary.

evidence.locator: Section 'Introduction', paragraph beginning 'First, AI will influence central banks' core activities'
evidence.passage: AI will affect financial systems as well as productivity, consumption, investment and labour markets, which themselves have direct effects on price and financial stability.
These developments are therefore of paramount concern to central banks.

missing: The passage links AI agents with blockchain-based services but does not state that AI agents' transactions would use, require or favour tokenised money or stablecoins, nor a consequence for the monetary system; the speech's later discussion of tokenised central bank money does not mention AI.
statement: In remarks of 3 March 2026, UEDA Kazuo, Governor of the Bank of Japan, said that integrating AI and blockchain is hoped to allow enhanced financial services using transaction and settlement data on blockchains, giving as examples financial advisory services via an AI agent and automated collateral valuation and substitution.
qualification: A statement of hopes for AI-blockchain integration in a speech on central bank money as an anchor of trust.

evidence.locator: Section on AI and blockchain, paragraph beginning 'Shifting our focus to AI'
evidence.passage: It is hoped that integrating AI and blockchain will allow the provision of enhanced financial services that utilize transaction and settlement data accumulated on the blockchain. Examples of this include provision of financial advisory services via an AI agent, automation of value assessments and substitutions of collateral

statement: Chapter 3 of the IMF Global Financial Stability Report of October 2024, prepared by IMF staff, states that AI provides opportunities for supervisors to automate data quality checks and help financial sector authorities detect anomalies in trading patterns.
qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy.

evidence.locator: Section "Best Practices", paragraph beginning "AI is providing numerous opportunities" (HTML)
evidence.passage: AI is providing numerous opportunities for supervisors to generate efficiency gains by automating data quality checks to ensure completeness, correctness, and consistency.

statement: The Basel Committee's newsletter of 16 March 2022 states that AI/ML models may be more difficult to manage than traditional models because they can be more complex, and names the extent to which model outcomes can be understood and explained as an area for continued discussion.
qualification: Informational; not supervisory guidance.

evidence.locator: Second paragraph of the main text, beginning 'In its discussions to date'
evidence.passage: In some cases, AI/ML models may be more difficult to manage than traditional models as they can be more complex.

evidence.locator: First of the three areas listed for continuing discussions
evidence.passage: The first area named for continuing discussions is the extent and degree to which the outcomes of models can be understood and explained.

statement: The FSB report of 27 June 2017 on financial stability implications from FinTech states, in its case study on AI and machine learning, that key potential benefits include applications of AI and machine learning in supervision, and that AI and machine learning can aid supervision by identifying new relationships in data.
qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The annex describes its findings as preliminary.

evidence.locator: Annex G, "Potential to support financial stability", PDF p. 60 (printed p. 56)
evidence.passage: Key potential benefits include various applications of AI and machine learning in supervision, internal audit and regulatory reporting, as well as the ability to better monitor risks.
AI and machine learning can aid supervision by allowing the identification of new relationships in data, without the filter of pre-specified models.
There is also a close link with “SupTech,” or the use of FinTech by supervisory authorities.
evidence.note: A glossary definition that does not mention AI; recorded only for the earliest located use of the name (audit, 2026-11-02).

engagement.rationale: The plan calls for AI-specific regulatory rules and laws for financial applications of AI without discussing whether existing financial rules already apply.

statement: The People's Bank of China's FinTech Development Plan 2019–2021 (August 2019) sets tasks to research and formulate regulatory rules for AI financial applications and to promote the establishment of laws and regulations, ethical norms and a policy system for AI financial applications.
qualification: Planned tasks, not adopted rules; the text does not state that existing rules are insufficient. English renderings are paraphrases.

evidence.locator: 第三章 重点任务, 第二节, item （六）稳步应用人工智能, PDF p. 14 (printed p. 14)
evidence.passage: 健全人工智能金融应用安全监测预警机制，研究制定人工智能金融应用监管规则，强化智能化金融工具安全认证
evidence.note: English paraphrase: improve the security monitoring and early-warning mechanism for AI financial applications, research and formulate regulatory rules for AI financial applications, and strengthen security certification of intelligent financial tools.

evidence.passage: 推动建立人工智能金融应用法律法规、伦理规范和政策体系
evidence.note: English paraphrase: promote the establishment of laws and regulations, ethical norms and a policy system for AI financial applications.

statement: Chapter 3 of the IMF Global Financial Stability Report of October 2024, prepared by IMF staff, states that fraud, disinformation and deepfakes will likely become more sophisticated as AI advances and could be used to manipulate financial markets and asset prices.
qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy.

evidence.locator: Section "Summarizing the Financial Stability Challenges", "Increased market manipulation and cyber risks" (HTML)
evidence.passage: Fraud, disinformation, and deepfakes will likely become more sophisticated as AI advances and could be used by bad actors to manipulate financial markets and asset prices.

statement: The FSB report of 1 November 2017 states that AI and machine-learning services are increasingly offered by a few large technology firms, that third-party dependencies could give rise to new systemically important players, and that these dependencies could have systemic effects if such a firm faced a major disruption or insolvency.
qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The report frames these as possible future developments ("may in the future").

evidence.passage: the emergence of a relatively small number of advanced third-party providers in AI and machine learning could increase concentration of some functions in the financial system.
AI and machine learning services are increasingly being offered by a few large technology firms.
These third-party dependencies and interconnections could have systemic effects if such a large firm were to face a major disruption or insolvency.

statement: The EIOPA Opinion on AI governance and risk management of 6 August 2025 states that AI systems in insurance that are neither prohibited nor high-risk under the AI Act continue to operate under existing sectoral legislation without new requirements, and that the Opinion sets out no new requirements but guidance on interpreting existing insurance legislation for AI systems.
qualification: The scope excludes prohibited and high-risk AI systems, which fall under the EU AI Act, an AI-specific law; the record concerns insurance sectoral legislation only.

evidence.passage: continue to operate subject to existing sectoral legislation without new requirements
This Opinion does not set out new requirements … This Opinion provides guidance on how to interpret various provisions of the existing insurance sectoral legislation in the context of AI systems

statement: In a speech of 29 September 2025, Christopher J. Waller, Governor of the Federal Reserve Board, said that AI can further improve the efficiency of payments, including through agentic AI executing tasks on behalf of a person or company quickly and cheaply through AI agents.
qualification: A brief statement within a speech mainly on distributed ledgers and stablecoins; it does not describe how payment systems would change. The speaker's view with disclaimer. His speech of 20 August 2025 called agentic AI 'the next wave' for payments innovators without stating that agents make payments (see searchLog).

evidence.locator: Section 'Assessing benefits of the next frontier of innovations', paragraph beginning 'Let's turn from DLT to AI'
evidence.passage: AI can further improve the efficiency of payments in a number of ways, including through automating manual tasks, detecting fraud or compliance risks, and now with agentic AI, executing tasks on behalf of a person or company quickly and cheaply through the use of AI agents.

statement: In a speech of 4 June 2019, James Proudman, Executive Director of UK Deposit Takers Supervision at the Bank of England, said that AI and machine learning are helping firms in anti-money laundering and fraud detection and that machine learning may also improve the quality of credit risk assessments.
qualification: The speech relies in part on survey evidence from firms and an IIF survey; it also turns to the risks. Not an evaluation of firms’ risk outcomes.

evidence.passage: For example, AI and ML are helping firms in anti-money laundering (AML) and fraud detection.
ML may also improve the quality of credit risk assessments, particularly for high-volume retail lending

statement: The FSB report of 1 November 2017 states that predictable patterns in the behaviour of automated trading strategies could be used by insiders or cybercriminals to manipulate market prices, and that uses of AI and machine learning should be assessed for risks including cybersecurity.
qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The manipulation passage concerns automated trading strategies, in a section on AI and machine learning in markets.

evidence.passage: advanced optimisation techniques and predictable patterns in the behaviour of automated trading strategies could be used by insiders or by cybercriminals to manipulate market prices.
It will be important to assess uses of AI and machine learning in view of their risks, including adherence to relevant protocols on data privacy, conduct risks, and cybersecurity.

statement: In a speech of 13 November 2018, Lael Brainard, then a member of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, said that existing regulatory and supervisory guardrails are a good place to start in assessing the approach to AI, naming the Federal Reserve's model risk management guidance (SR 11-7) and vendor risk management guidance as relevant to AI tools.
qualification: A starting point rather than a conclusion: she also says the Federal Reserve is 'still learning' and welcomes discussion of how existing laws and guidance intersect with AI. The speaker's view with disclaimer, not Board guidance.

evidence.locator: Section 'Current Regulatory and Supervisory Approaches', paragraph beginning 'It is incumbent on regulators'
evidence.passage: Our existing regulatory and supervisory guardrails are a good place to start as we assess the appropriate approach for AI processes.

evidence.locator: Same section, paragraph beginning 'Second, our guidance on vendor risk management'
evidence.passage: could be expected to apply as well to AI-based tools or services that are externally sourced.

engagement.rationale: Disputes that existing frameworks suffice in specific areas (governance, skills, explainability, data, new players and the third-party perimeter), while not calling for a separate AI framework.

statement: FSI Insights No 63 of December 2024, by Crisanto, Leuterio, Prenio and Yong, states that AI use may present unique challenges so that regulatory or supervisory guidance may be needed in specific areas, and that provider concentration strengthens the argument for direct oversight frameworks for cloud and AI service providers.
qualification: A partial contest within a text that also articulates U12; the paper says authorities 'may need to examine existing regulations and, if needed, issue clarifications, revisions or even new regulations' in listed areas.

evidence.passage: Nevertheless, AI use by financial institutions may present some unique challenges and hence regulatory or supervisory guidance may be needed in specific areas.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 2), executive summary, bullet 'Regulatory perimeter – third parties'
evidence.passage: The concentration of cloud and AI service providers to a few large global technology firms strengthens the argument for putting in place direct oversight frameworks for these service providers depending on available legal authority.
evidence.note: Same passage as in am-u02-fsi-2024-insights-63; counted once.

statement: In a speech of 7 November 2025, Philip N. Jefferson, Vice Chair of the Federal Reserve Board, said that productivity gains from AI may affect the relationship between employment and inflation and hence the conduct of monetary policy, while adding that it is likely still too soon to tell what these effects mean for policy.
qualification: The speaker's view with disclaimer, stated with explicit uncertainty; no policy action is proposed.
